demographics: More common in people with a long smoking history
In the US, prevalence is higher among adults with lower income and less education
Slightly more common in men, largely reflecting historical smoking patterns

risk_factors.text: Occupational exposure to dusts, fumes, or chemical vapors
Family history of COPD in a smoker

social_history: Cigarette smoking, often 20 or more pack-years
Exposure to secondhand smoke at home or work
Work in mining, construction, manufacturing, farming, or other dusty trades

chief_complaints.text: I've had a cough with phlegm for months and it won't go away
I get winded just walking up the stairs
My chest feels tight and I wheeze

hpi.onset: Gradual, over years; most people first notice the cough in their 40s or later
hpi.duration: Cough and sputum on most days for at least 3 months a year, for 2 years or more
hpi.progression: Slowly worsening; cough and sputum come first, then breathlessness with activity, then breathlessness with minimal activity as the disease advances
hpi.quality: Loose, rattling cough that brings up sputum; chest tightness; breathlessness on exertion
hpi.severity: Mild at first and easy to dismiss as a 'smoker's cough'; becomes moderate to severe over years
hpi.timing: Cough is worst in the morning right after waking and when lying down; symptoms are worse in cold air and during respiratory infections
aggravating: Smoke, dust, fumes, or strong odors

associated_symptoms.text: Cough that brings up clear, white, or gray sputum
Wheezing or a whistling sound when breathing
Sputum that turns yellow or green during flare-ups
Waking at night coughing or short of breath
Ankle or leg swelling in advanced disease
Unintentional weight loss in advanced disease

pertinent_negatives: Fever with the chronic cough between flare-ups
Sudden severe shortness of breath at rest
Sharp chest pain that worsens with a deep breath
Leg pain or swelling in one calf only
Weight loss before the illness became severe
New wheezing that started in childhood or as a young adult
Symptoms that began suddenly over hours to days

positives.text: Ankle or leg swelling in advanced disease

argues_against: Heart failure as the primary cause
Gastroesophageal reflux as the sole cause of cough

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to 'just getting older' or to heart disease, and activity limitation may be the main complaint rather than cough.
Chronic bronchitis is uncommon in children; a chronic productive cough in a child should prompt evaluation for asthma, cystic fibrosis, or recurrent aspiration instead.
Increasing shortness of breath may be attributed to normal pregnancy changes, delaying recognition of worsening lung disease.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal link to smoking history

atypical.how_it_differs: Recurrent chest infections may dominate the picture and the chronic cough may be attributed to infection rather than underlying airway disease.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, speaks in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Speaks in full sentences but pauses to breathe when walking or climbing; mild tachypnea
general.severe: Sits upright, pursed-lip breathing, uses accessory muscles, speaks in short phrases
general.critical: Ill-appearing, tripod position, unable to speak in full sentences, may be confused or somnolent

labs.caveat: Mild normocytic anemia of chronic disease; a low MCV should prompt iron studies and consideration of chronic blood loss.
Normal between exacerbations; leukocytosis suggests a superimposed bacterial infection or another cause.
Eosinophilia is more typical of asthma than of COPD; a high count should prompt reconsideration.
A rising bicarbonate is a clue to chronic CO2 retention and should prompt an arterial blood gas.
Hypercapnia with a normal pH indicates chronic compensated retention; a low pH means acute-on-chronic respiratory failure.
Acidemia in a patient with chronic bronchitis means acute respiratory failure and is an escalation trigger.
Ordered when heart failure is a competing explanation for dyspnea; values are lower than in acute decompensated heart failure but can be mildly elevated from right heart strain.
Rises during exacerbations; not useful for diagnosis of stable disease.
Low values argue against bacterial infection and can support withholding antibiotics during an exacerbation.
Comorbidity screening; also relevant because systemic steroids during exacerbations worsen glycemia.

ST depression in the inferior and lateral leads from right heart strain
T wave inversion in the right precordial leads

No filling defect; right ventricular enlargement from chronic lung disease

criteria.name: Clinical definition of chronic bronchitis
criteria.summary: A chronic productive cough on most days for at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years, with other causes of chronic cough excluded.
items: Productive cough present on most days
No alternative explanation for the cough

criteria.name: COPD airflow obstruction on spirometry
criteria.summary: Persistent airflow obstruction demonstrated by a reduced post-bronchodilator FEV1 to FVC ratio.
items: Severity graded by FEV1 percent predicted
Symptoms and exposure history consistent with COPD

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, wheeze, and chest tightness with reversible airflow obstruction

history: Symptoms often begin in childhood or young adulthood
Episodic attacks with symptom-free intervals
Worse at night and with allergens, exercise, or cold air
Personal or family history of atopy, eczema, or allergic rhinitis
exam: Wheezing during exacerbations with clear lungs between episodes
No chronic sputum production between attacks
labs: Elevated total IgE or positive allergen-specific IgE

differential.name: Heart failure
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea on exertion, cough, wheeze, and leg swelling in an older adult
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or bilateral crackles that do not clear with coughing

history: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Chest pain or known coronary disease
Rapid weight gain from fluid retention
exam: Bibasilar crackles that persist after coughing
Elevated jugular venous pressure
S3 gallop
Cool extremities or narrow pulse pressure in advanced disease
imaging: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary venous congestion, or pleural effusions on chest x-ray
Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction on echocardiogram

differential.name: Lung cancer
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough in a long-term smoker, sometimes with sputum changes
differential.trigger: Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, hoarseness, or a new focal finding on chest imaging

history: Hemoptysis
Unintentional weight loss
Hoarseness or dysphagia
Symptoms that progress despite inhaler therapy
exam: Focal wheeze that does not clear with coughing
Digital clubbing
Supraclavicular or cervical lymphadenopathy
Horner syndrome or superior vena cava findings in advanced disease
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase if bone metastases
imaging: Solitary pulmonary nodule, mass, or hilar adenopathy on chest x-ray
Enlarging or spiculated mass on CT

differential.name: Bronchiectasis
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough with daily purulent sputum

history: Large volumes of purulent sputum daily
Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe
History of severe childhood respiratory infection or measles
Hemoptysis
exam: Coarse crackles at the lung bases
Halitosis
labs: Sputum culture growing Pseudomonas aeruginosa or nontuberculous mycobacteria
imaging: Dilated airways with a signet-ring appearance and tram-track lines on high-resolution CT

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough with sputum in a patient with risk factors
differential.trigger: Night sweats, fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or known exposure to tuberculosis

history: Night sweats and low-grade fever
Unintentional weight loss
Immigration from or travel to a high-prevalence country
Incarceration, shelter residence, or HIV infection
exam: Upper-lobe crackles or amphoric breath sounds
Lymphadenopathy
labs: Positive interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test
Positive nucleic acid amplification test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
imaging: Upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or miliary pattern on chest x-ray
Tree-in-bud nodularity and cavitary lesions on CT

differential.name: Upper airway cough syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough that is worse when lying down and improves with antihistamines

history: Postnasal drip and frequent throat clearing
Nasal congestion and sneezing
Cough is the only or predominant symptom
Improves with intranasal steroids or antihistamines
exam: Cobblestoning of the posterior pharynx
Clear nasal discharge or mucosal swelling

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough worsened by lying flat and by meals

history: Heartburn and regurgitation
Cough worse after meals and when supine
Improves with proton pump inhibitor therapy
exam: Normal lung examination
No wheezing

differential.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
differential.why_considered: COPD with chronic bronchitis in a younger patient or with minimal smoking exposure

history: COPD before age 45
Minimal or no smoking history
Family history of early emphysema or liver disease
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or a relative
exam: Early-onset emphysema with basilar predominance
Signs of liver disease in some patients
labs: PI*ZZ or other deficient genotype on phenotyping or genotyping

severity.mild: Chronic productive cough on most days with preserved exercise tolerance; FEV1 at or above 80% predicted; SpO2 94% or higher at rest; no signs of right heart failure
severity.moderate: Daily cough and sputum with dyspnea on moderate exertion such as climbing one flight of stairs; FEV1 50 to 79% predicted; SpO2 90 to 95%; occasional exacerbations
severity.severe: Dyspnea with minimal activity or at rest; FEV1 30 to 49% predicted; SpO2 85 to 92%; frequent exacerbations; may have peripheral edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, or polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia
severity.critical: Acute-on-chronic respiratory failure with acidemia, hypercapnia, and hypoxemia; altered mental status; inability to speak in full sentences; hemodynamic instability; requires noninvasive or invasive ventilation

red_flags.finding: Acidemia on arterial blood gas in a patient with known CO2 retention
red_flags.meaning: Acute-on-chronic respiratory failure; needs urgent ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status, somnolence, or asterixis
SpO2 below 88% on room air or new oxygen requirement
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; assess for pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, or pneumothorax
Consider lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or tuberculosis rather than uncomplicated chronic bronchitis

red_flags.finding: Unilateral leg swelling or pleuritic chest pain
Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain with absent breath sounds
red_flags.meaning: Pneumothorax, which is more common in patients with emphysema

red_flags.finding: Fever with purulent sputum and worsening dyspnea
red_flags.meaning: Acute bacterial exacerbation or pneumonia; needs antibiotics and possibly hospitalization

red_flags.finding: New focal wheeze or focal crackles
red_flags.meaning: Consider endobronchial obstruction from a mass or a retained foreign body

complications.name: Cor pulmonale and right heart failure
Pneumothorax
clues: Absent breath sounds on one side

complications.name: Pulmonary hypertension
clues: Exertional dyspnea out of proportion to spirometry
Prominent central pulmonary arteries on chest x-ray

special_populations.differences: Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or heart disease; activity limitation may be the presenting complaint rather than cough. Comorbid heart failure and coronary disease are common and can mimic or worsen dyspnea.
Increasing dyspnea may be attributed to normal pregnancy changes, delaying recognition of worsening lung disease. Smoking cessation support is a priority; hypoxemia threatens both mother and fetus.

Recurrent chest infections may dominate the picture and the chronic cough may be attributed to infection rather than underlying airway disease. Consider atypical organisms and evaluate for bronchiectasis.
Reduced chest wall compliance and deconditioning worsen dyspnea; obesity hypoventilation can add to CO2 retention and complicate interpretation of blood gases.
Systemic corticosteroids used during exacerbations cause hyperglycemia; monitor glucose closely and adjust therapy.

key_questions.question: How long have you had this cough, and does it bring up phlegm?
key_questions.looking_for: Productive cough on most days for at least 3 months a year for 2 or more years

key_questions.question: Is the cough there every day, or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic daily pattern rather than episodic attacks with symptom-free intervals

key_questions.question: When during the day is the cough worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Worst in the morning after waking and when lying down

key_questions.question: What does the sputum look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear, white, or gray most days; yellow or green during flare-ups

key_questions.question: Do you get short of breath? With what level of activity?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional dyspnea that has crept in after years of cough; grades activity tolerance

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you ever smoked? How much and for how many years?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or former cigarette use, often 20 or more pack-years

key_questions.question: Have you been exposed to dusts, fumes, or chemicals at work, or to secondhand smoke at home?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or household inhaled irritants that add to the smoking risk

key_questions.question: Have you coughed up any blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hemoptysis points to cancer, bronchiectasis, or tuberculosis

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight without trying, or had night sweats or fevers between flare-ups?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests malignancy, tuberculosis, or another chronic infection

key_questions.question: Do you wake up at night short of breath, or need extra pillows to sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to heart failure

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your ankles or legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral swelling in advanced disease suggests cor pulmonale; one-sided swelling suggests DVT

key_questions.question: How many chest colds or flare-ups have you had in the past year, and have you needed antibiotics or steroids?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent exacerbations, which drive management and prognosis

key_questions.question: What inhalers or other breathing medicines do you use, and do they help?
key_questions.looking_for: Bronchodilator use with partial relief; steroid inhalers in more severe disease

key_questions.question: Have you had your flu and pneumococcal vaccines?
Does anyone in your family have COPD, emphysema, or liver disease at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

key_questions.question: Has your cough changed recently, or is it worse than it has ever been?
key_questions.looking_for: A change in a stable chronic pattern, which should prompt evaluation for a new problem

reasoning_points: Productive cough on most days for at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years
Other causes of chronic cough excluded (asthma, upper airway cough syndrome, reflux, infection, malignancy)
Long-term cigarette smoke exposure, often 20 or more pack-years
Typical age of onset in the 40s or later, with gradual worsening over years
Cough worst in the morning and with cold air or infections
Spirometry showing persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction with FEV1/FVC below 0.70
Chest imaging without a mass, infiltrate, or other alternative explanation
No hemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, or fever between flare-ups

easy: Long-time smoker over 40 with a daily morning productive cough for years
Sputum is clear to white and worse in the morning
Diffuse expiratory wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase on exam
medium: Patient dismisses the cough as a 'smoker's cough' and reports only exertional dyspnea
Coexisting heart failure or asthma makes the cause of dyspnea ambiguous
Older adult whose activity limitation is attributed to aging
Chest x-ray is normal, which does not exclude the diagnosis
hard: Younger patient or one with minimal smoking history, raising concern for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Chronic cough with purulent sputum and recurrent same-lobe pneumonias suggesting bronchiectasis
Smoker with hemoptysis or weight loss requiring evaluation for lung cancer
Acute-on-chronic presentation with hypercapnia and acidemia obscuring the underlying chronic disease
Immunocompromised patient whose recurrent infections dominate the picture
